title: Bayesian Influence Functions for Hessian-Free Data Attribution
claim: A classical influence measure based on Hessian inversion can be replaced by covariance statistics over the local loss landscape, retaining higher-order geometry.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, formulas on top, equivalence arrow between panels (b) and (c)
description: Three panels read left to right. Panel (a) is a 3D loss-landscape surface in red-to-blue gradient. It has a deep blue basin and jagged red walls, and a flat contour map sits beneath it. Panel (b) is a flat diamond with concentric blue contours. Red gradient arrows for samples i and j sit next to a black H+γI marker. The formula IF = ⟨∇ℓi, ∇ℓj⟩ with (H+γI)^-1 sits above it. Two annotations say the Hessian is intractable and that dampening masks higher-order interactions. Panel (c) is a diamond with a star-shaped contour pattern and a dense cloud of SGLD samples. The formula BIF = Cov_γ[ℓi, ℓj] sits above it. Annotations say that gradient-based MCMC enables batched estimation and that a Gaussian prior retains sensitivity to degeneracy. A curved arrow labelled 'asymptotically equivalent in the absence of degeneracy' links (c) back to (b). Bold captions sit below each panel.
caption: From influence functions (IF) to Bayesian influence functions (BIF): We introduce the local Bayesian Influence Function (BIF), which replaces the Hessian inversion of classical Influence Functions (IF) with a covariance estimation over the local loss landscape. This approach is sensitive to higher-order geometry and scales to models with billions of parameters.
abstract: Classical influence functions face significant challenges when applied to deep neural networks, primarily due to non-invertible Hessians and high-dimensional parameter spaces. We propose the local Bayesian influence function (BIF), an extension of classical influence functions that replaces Hessian inversion with loss landscape statistics that can be estimated via stochastic-gradient MCMC sampling. This Hessian-free approach captures higher-order interactions among parameters and scales efficiently to neural networks with billions of parameters. We demonstrate state-of-the-art results on predicting retraining experiments.
